mainEntity.name: Do you supply products or only introduce factories?

acceptedAnswer.text: Our offer is product sourcing, purchase and supply. The company identified in your quotation contracts with you and invoices the products. Specifications, samples, product pricing and order responsibilities are agreed before you commit.

mainEntity.name: Do you only source clothing and packaging?

acceptedAnswer.text: Clothing, textiles and packaging are our core specialties. We also source other products on request, after reviewing the product, quantity, specifications and production requirements.

mainEntity.name: Can I start a sourcing project now?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. We can work on projects and invoice from France or China now, supported by an established independent China sourcing partnership. The contracting company is identified in your quotation. The planned Miami expansion in 2027 does not prevent you from starting a project today.

mainEntity.name: Can you work from an existing design or sample?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Send your brief, reference images, dimensions, quantity, and target timing. We will confirm what can be quoted and sampled.

mainEntity.name: Who handles compliance and import requirements?

acceptedAnswer.text: Requirements depend on the exact product and destination. Product specifications, certificates, shipping terms, and importer responsibilities are confirmed for each order before production and shipment.

mainEntity.name: Which company will invoice my order?

acceptedAnswer.text: Current projects are contracted and invoiced through a company in France or China, identified in your quotation before you commit. Product specifications, pricing, samples, payment terms and delivery responsibilities are agreed for each order. The U.S. expansion remains planned.

mainEntity.name: What is the minimum order quantity?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single minimum order quantity for every product. Materials, construction, finishes and quantities by size, color or artwork affect the proposal. Send your brief so we can review the available options.

acceptedAnswer.text: An agent acts on your behalf and is paid for the service, while you buy from the factory. pages.content: September 7, 2026China Sourcing RFQ Checklist: How to Prepare a Product BriefBy Gregory BaranesPrepare a China sourcing quotation request with product specs, quantities, samples and delivery requirements. Includes a free brief template.A useful China sourcing request for quotation (RFQ) identifies the product, intended use, specifications, quantity by variant, sample requirements, destination and target date. Separate requirements you must keep from details you can change. This gives the supplier or product supply partner a clear basis for assessing feasibility and preparing a proposal. Download the free product sourcing brief template. Fill in what you know and mark unresolved details as “to confirm.” The template works for clothing, packaging and other products submitted for feasibility review.What should a sourcing brief include?Give each product its own reference number. Include these details in the same document: Product and use: what it is, who will use it, and how it will be sold or used. Reference material: drawings, photographs, a tech pack, a dieline or an existing sample. Identify which details are for inspiration and which must be reproduced. Specification: materials, dimensions, colors, construction, decoration and packaging. State units and tolerances where known. Quantity: total units and the breakdown by style, size, color, artwork or other variant. Separate a first order from a possible repeat order. Sample review: which features need approval before production and who will approve them. Commercial target: budget, currency and what you expect that budget to include. Mark estimates clearly. Destination and timing: delivery location, target arrival date, and whether that date is flexible. Required documentation: documents or product claims your team needs to review before approving the order. Do not fill gaps with guesses. An unanswered specification is something to resolve; an incorrect specification can become the basis of a quotation.What is different for clothing and textiles?For a garment, include front and back drawings, a size chart, fabric composition and weight, color references, stitching, trims, labels and decoration placement. Break quantities down by size and color. Say whether a reference garment represents the fit, the fabric, the finish, or all three. For a tote bag or another textile item, dimensions, construction, intended use and decoration may matter more than a garment size chart. A reference photo alone rarely describes every detail needed for production. The apparel tech pack and MOQ guide explains how to discuss materials and order quantities. See the clothing and textile sourcing page for the product scope.What is different for custom packaging?Start with the product being packed. Include its dimensions, weight, fragility, presentation needs and intended packing method. Specify whether box measurements are internal or external. If you have a dieline, include its revision and the artwork files associated with it. Describe the structure, material, print, finish, inserts and closure. State whether different artwork versions share the same structure. Ask for a sample that lets you check product fit as well as appearance. Explore custom packaging sourcing, private label packaging and the packaging MOQ guide.How do you compare product quotations?Compare proposals against the same brief and revision. For each quotation, record the unit price, quantity, included materials and finishes, sample charges, setup or tooling costs, payment terms, quotation validity and delivery basis. Ask what is excluded. Check whether an alternative material, different quantity or simpler finish explains a price difference. Keep proposed substitutions separate from the original specification until you approve them. Sample timing, production timing and transport timing should be identified separately. A production estimate alone does not confirm the date goods will arrive at your destination. For a cost worksheet, use the landed-cost planning guide.What should be confirmed before production?Keep an approval record linking the final specification, approved sample, quantity breakdown and commercial terms. Identify the production checkpoints, how changes will be approved and who is responsible for each delivery step. Requirements for testing, documentation or import review depend on the exact product and should be settled with the appropriate parties before the order proceeds. A quotation request is the start of a conversation. It is not an order confirmation, a fixed price or a guarantee that a product can be supplied.How will Sourcing Lab USA use your brief?Sourcing Lab USA accepts China sourcing projects now, with invoicing from France or China as identified in the quotation. Clothing, textiles and packaging are the core specialties; other products are assessed on request through an established independent China sourcing partnership. The quotation identifies the company in France or China purchasing, supplying and invoicing the products, along with the commercial terms. The brief helps define what can be proposed, sampled and agreed before an order. Read about China-to-U.S. product sourcing and supply, or send your project brief. pages.content: September 3, 2026Apparel Sourcing: Understanding Tech Packs and MOQBy Gregory BaranesUpdated September 8, 2026Learn why a clear tech pack is essential for negotiating Minimum Order Quantities (MOQ) and defining product requirements when sourcing custom textiles.When U.S. brands start sourcing custom apparel and textiles from China, two terms immediately dominate the conversation: Tech Packs and MOQ (Minimum Order Quantity). A tech pack records the product specification; MOQ is the minimum quantity quoted for a particular product or variant. Review them together, because materials, colors, construction and setup requirements can affect the quantity a supplier can propose.What is a Tech Pack?A Tech Pack (Technical Packet) is the blueprint for your textile product. It is a comprehensive document that contains every detail a factory needs to manufacture your garment or textile item. A standard tech pack includes: Technical Sketches: Flat drawings of the front, back, and details. Bill of Materials (BOM): A list of all fabrics, threads, buttons, zippers, and labels required. Measurements and Grading: Exact dimensions for every size you plan to produce. Construction Details: Stitching types, seam finishes, and placement of labels. Colorways: Specific Pantone codes or color references. Why the Tech Pack Dictates the MOQMany brands ask, "What is your standard MOQ?" before providing any product details. The reality is that for custom textiles, the MOQ is rarely a fixed number—it is determined by the details in your tech pack. Here is why: Fabric Minimums (MOQ of the Mill): If your tech pack specifies a custom-dyed fabric or a unique blend, the factory must purchase that fabric from a mill. Ask whether fabric minimums apply to the proposed material and color, and how those minimums affect the garment quantity. Setup Costs: Custom hardware (like branded zippers) or complex printing (like all-over sublimation) requires significant setup time. Factories require higher MOQs to absorb these setup costs. How to Lower Your MOQ Using Your Tech PackIf you are a startup or testing a new product line, you likely want to keep your MOQ as low as possible. You can design your tech pack strategically to achieve this: Use Available Market Fabrics: Instead of custom-dying a fabric to a specific Pantone color, ask your sourcing partner to find an "available market fabric" (in-stock fabric) that closely matches your requirement. This may change the minimum commitment; availability and quantities still need confirmation. Standardize Hardware: Use standard buttons and zippers rather than custom-molded hardware. Consolidate Colors: Launch with one or two core colors rather than five different colorways. MOQs are often calculated per color, per style. The Importance of a Clear BriefA detailed tech pack helps identify assumptions before an order is approved. When a factory has to guess your requirements, they price in risk, which often results in higher costs and stricter MOQs. By presenting a professional, complete specification, you demonstrate that you are a serious buyer, which can give you more leverage during negotiations. Sourcing projects are available now, with contracting and invoicing from France or China as identified in your quotation. pages.content: September 3, 2026Sustainable Packaging Sourcing: Materials, Claims and a Better BriefBy Gregory BaranesUpdated September 8, 2026Turn packaging sustainability goals into specific material and documentation requirements. Compare options for protection, structure and supported claims.A useful sustainable packaging brief specifies a measurable goal: less material, a documented recycled-content requirement, or a design intended for a particular disposal route. Describe the complete package and request evidence for any claim you plan to make. A material name or natural-looking finish is not enough to substantiate an environmental benefit.Start with the goal and the productRecord the product dimensions, weight, protection needs, presentation requirements and how the customer will use the packaging. Then identify the environmental objective. Keep product protection and the intended packing process in the brief so proposed changes can be assessed against both. For example, you might ask to compare a current box and insert with a revised structure using fewer separate components. This is a comparison request, not a promise of reduced environmental impact or lower delivery costs.Specify the whole packaging structureList the board or paper, coatings, laminations, inks, adhesive, closures and inserts. Ask suppliers to identify proposed substitutions. Compare the complete construction; one component does not describe the finished package. For recycled-content requirements, state the component the requirement applies to and request the supporting documentation. Keep certification requests specific to the material, supplier and production route being proposed.Check the claim before printing itThe FTC Green Guides summary cautions against broad, unqualified environmental benefit claims and explains how specific claims need support. Recyclability and recycled content are different claims; do not treat one as proof of the other. Before adding an environmental statement to artwork, obtain an appropriate review of the wording and evidence. Describe which part of the product or package the statement covers. Sourcing Lab USA does not act as a certification body.Compare samples and commercial termsReview product fit, assembly, appearance and protection using the agreed sample process. For each option, record the dimensions, materials, unit price, quantity, setup charges and packing details. Ask how a proposed change affects the specification and shipment configuration rather than assuming savings. Keep the final material specification, supporting documents and artwork approval together. If any component changes before production, review whether the original claim and approval still apply.Prepare a packaging sourcing requestSourcing Lab USA welcomes product sourcing projects now, with invoicing from France or China as confirmed in the quotation. A clear brief helps assess custom packaging options through its independent China sourcing partnership. Material choices, samples, documentation and commercial terms are confirmed per project. pages.content: August 28, 2026Custom Packaging MOQ: How to Plan a First Production RunBy Gregory BaranesUpdated August 31, 2026Understand the factors that shape a custom packaging minimum order quantity and the information to confirm before you request a quote.Moving from stock packaging to a fully customized product creates a new question: what is the minimum order quantity, or MOQ? There is no universal answer. The workable MOQ depends on the item, material, printing method, finish, tooling, dimensions, and supplier's production setup. The most useful starting point is a clear brief rather than a target quantity in isolation.Why MOQs varyCustom packaging may require setup steps before the first production unit is made. Depending on the project, these can include artwork preparation, color matching, printing setup, cutting or forming tools, material purchasing, and hand assembly. A supplier needs a production run that makes those steps viable. Two boxes that look similar can have very different MOQs if one uses standard dimensions and a simple print while the other needs a new structure, special material, detailed finish, or several assembly steps.Questions to include in your RFQAsk the supplier to state: MOQ for the quoted specification; price breaks at practical quantities; one-time tooling or setup charges; sample cost and timing; included and excluded finishing steps; carton details, production lead time, and shipping terms. Ways to explore a lower commitmentIf the first MOQ is too high for the project, consider options that preserve the product objective: Use a standard structure or size where it still protects the product. Compare a simpler finish or printing method with the initial concept. Separate the first sample run from production quantities. Ask for quantity breakpoints and compare total order cost, not only unit price. Sourcing Lab USA can review a custom packaging brief, including the specification, estimated quantity, sample needs, and delivery destination, before coordinating supplier proposals. The final MOQ and commercial terms are confirmed for each order. For a complete packaging brief, see custom packaging for U.S. brands. pages.content: August 25, 2026How to Discuss Material Claims When Sourcing Custom TextilesBy Gregory BaranesUpdated August 31, 2026A practical way to define textile material requirements, request supporting documents, and avoid making claims that the order cannot substantiate.When a custom textile project includes organic, recycled, or other material claims, the specification has to be more precise than a marketing phrase. The fiber blend, construction, color, trims, labels, intended use, and documentation requirements can all affect the supplier options, sampling process, price, and lead time. This article is a sourcing checklist, not a certification or compliance opinion. Requirements should be assessed for the particular product and market before production.Start with a material briefDescribe the product in a way that a supplier can quote consistently: fiber composition and target weight; weave, knit, construction, size, and tolerances; color, printing, embroidery, labels, and trims; intended use and target market; quantity, target delivery date, and any documents the buyer needs to review. Compare like-for-like optionsMaterial choices can change the cost, minimum order quantity, performance, appearance, and production lead time. Instead of assuming a fixed premium, request comparable proposals for the same specification and quantity. Make clear which elements are mandatory and which can be adjusted after sampling.Request documentation before making a claimIf a buyer intends to make a certification, recycled-content, organic-content, or safety claim, request the relevant documentation from the proposed supplier and check that its scope and validity match the material and production route being quoted. Examples that may be relevant depending on the product include GOTS, GRS, and OEKO-TEX® STANDARD 100. Do not assume that a document applies to every component of a finished product. Where a claim matters commercially, obtain appropriate professional advice and retain the documents required for the order.Use sampling to confirm the productSampling is where the material hand feel, color, construction, print, trims, labeling, and packaging can be reviewed against the agreed brief. Record approved changes before production so that the final specification and commercial terms stay aligned. Sourcing Lab USA coordinates custom textile procurement around the specific brief, supplier proposal, samples, and agreed production follow-up. Documentation, quality checkpoints, shipping terms, and importer responsibilities are agreed case by case; the company does not represent itself as a certification body, testing laboratory, or customs adviser. pages.content: August 20, 2026How to Plan Landed Costs for Custom Packaging and Textile OrdersBy Gregory BaranesUpdated August 31, 2026A practical checklist of the cost items to confirm before ordering custom packaging or textiles from China to the United States.A factory quote is only one part of the purchase decision. For a custom packaging or textile order, the useful number is the landed cost: the total cost allocated to each unit once it reaches the agreed destination. The exact items, rates, and party responsible depend on the product, origin, Incoterm, shipment method, importer of record, and destination. Treat this as a planning checklist, not a customs or tax determination.What is Landed Cost?The landed cost is the combined cost of the goods and the services required to bring them to the delivery point agreed in the order. It should be calculated against the same quantity and delivery terms as the supplier quote. The Landed Cost Formula Landed Cost = Product cost + International transport + Insurance (if applicable) + Import charges + U.S. handling/delivery + Order-specific costs Before approving a production run, ask for each item to be shown separately whenever possible.1. Product and production costsConfirm the unit price, quantity, tooling or setup, sample charges, artwork changes, packaging of the finished goods, payment terms, and the Incoterm. A lower unit price can be less useful if it excludes an essential cost or only applies to a different specification.2. Transport and insuranceRequest a transport quote that matches the final carton count, dimensions, weight, pickup point, delivery point, and preferred shipping method. For both packaging and textiles, the way goods are packed can materially affect the chargeable volume. Insurance and delivery services should be stated separately if they are not included.3. Classification and import chargesProduct classification, duty treatment, tariffs, and import responsibilities must be checked against the exact product and current rules. The U.S. International Trade Commission's HTS is the official tariff schedule; when binding guidance is required, U.S. Customs and Border Protection explains how to request a classification ruling through its eRulings process. Do not rely on a generic rate or an AI estimate for an import decision. Confirm the classification, applicable charges, and importer obligations for the specific order. A customs broker may be used, but CBP notes that the importer remains responsible for the entry information and duties even when a broker is involved.4. U.S. handling and order-specific costsDepending on the agreed route and terms, the budget may also include port or terminal handling, domestic delivery, storage, inspections arranged by the buyer, or other order-specific services. These should be confirmed in the commercial terms rather than assumed.A practical review before you orderFor each project, build one written cost sheet showing what is included, excluded, estimated, and still to be verified. Sourcing Lab USA can review the product brief, specifications, sample needs, and supplier proposal for packaging and textile projects. Import, delivery, and compliance responsibilities are confirmed in the order-specific commercial terms. For project scope and order terms, see China-to-U.S. packaging and textile procurement. Landed cost depends on what you are buying and on what terms — China-to-U.S. procurement sets out how those terms are confirmed per order.

pages.content: FREE TEMPLATE · NO EMAIL REQUIREDThe product sourcing briefa supplier can actually quote.A product sourcing brief is the document a supplier quotes from. It states the product, the reference it must match, materials, dimensions, quantity by variant, sample and approval requirements, destination and target date, and separates what is mandatory from what can change. Anything unresolved is marked "to confirm" rather than guessed, because a guessed figure produces a quotation for the wrong product.Download the templateRead it on this pagePlain text, so it opens anywhere and pastes into an email. No sign-up, no tracking, nothing to accept.WHAT THE TEMPLATE ASKS FORSix sections, in the order a supplier reads them.Business and contactCompanyContact nameEmailProduct reference, brief revision and dateProductProduct descriptionIntended use and intended customerReference images, drawings, tech pack or dielineDetails that must match the referenceMaterials and compositionDimensions, units and tolerancesColours, artwork and finishesLabels, trims and packagingMandatory requirementsOptions open to changeQuantityFirst-order quantityBreakdown by size, style, colour or artworkPossible repeat quantity, as an estimate onlySamples and approvalSamples neededFeatures to reviewPerson approving the sampleDocuments or claims to reviewCommercial and deliveryBudget and currencyItems expected within the budgetDelivery destinationTarget arrival date and flexibilityProposed delivery terms, to confirmImport and delivery responsibilities, to confirmQuestions to resolveOutstanding specificationsProduct feasibilityMinimum order quantity by variantUnit price, sample and setup chargesQuotation validity and payment termsSample, production and transport timingProduction checkpoints and change approvalsWHAT TO PLAN AROUNDFigures to hold in mind while you fill it in.Minimum order quantityFrom 500 unitsA common starting point. The real minimum follows the product, material, construction, decoration and the split across sizes or colours.Samples1 to 2 weeksOnce the specification is agreed. A new mould, tooling or a custom material extends it, and a revised sample restarts the cycle.Production45 to 60 daysAfter sample approval, before shipping. Quantity, decoration and factory loading at the time of order all move it.Indicative planning figures, not commitments. The quantity, sampling scope and production timing for your project are confirmed in your quotation.WHAT MAKES A BRIEF UNANSWERABLEFour gaps that send a quotation off course.A quantity with no breakdownFive thousand units across one size behaves nothing like five thousand across six sizes and three colours. The breakdown is what decides whether a minimum is reachable.A reference with no boundaryAttaching a reference product without saying which parts must match leaves the supplier to guess. State what is fixed and what is open.A guessed figure instead of "to confirm"A placeholder dimension or material is treated as a requirement and quoted against. Marking it unresolved costs nothing and avoids a quotation for the wrong product.A claim with no evidence pathA performance, safety or compliance requirement needs to say what evidence will be accepted. It cannot be assumed from a fabric name or a reference product.QUESTIONS, ANSWEREDAbout the brief.What is a product sourcing brief?It is the document a supplier quotes from. It states the product, the reference it must match, materials and dimensions, quantity by variant, sample and approval requirements, destination and target date, and separates mandatory requirements from details that can change.What is the difference between a brief and an RFQ?In practice they are the same document seen from two sides. The brief describes the product you want made; the request for quotation asks a supplier what that product costs and how long it takes. One well-written brief serves as the RFQ.How complete does a brief need to be before sending it?It does not need to be complete. Mark what is unresolved as "to confirm" and send it. An incomplete brief with honest gaps gets a useful first answer; a brief filled with guessed figures gets a quotation for a product you did not intend.What quantities and timing should I plan around?As an indication, minimum order quantities commonly start around 500 units, samples take one to two weeks once the specification is agreed, and production runs about 45 to 60 days after sample approval. All three depend on the product and are confirmed in the quotation.

pages.content: Privacy noticeThis page explains what we collect when you use this website, why we collect it, where it is stored, and how to have it removed. Last updated 7 September 2026.What we collectWhen you send a project brief we collect your name, email address, the type of product you need, an approximate quantity, the page you sent the brief from, and — if you choose to provide them — your company name and a description of your project.If you join the product update list we collect your email address and the sourcing role you select.We do not ask for payment details, identity documents, or any special category of personal data anywhere on this site.Why we collect itA project brief is used to answer your request: to confirm what can be quoted and sampled, to ask for anything missing, and to reply to you by email. Product update registrations are used only to send occasional updates about the service.We do not sell your information, we do not share it with advertising networks, and we do not add you to a marketing sequence because you sent a brief.Where it is storedBriefs and product update registrations are stored in a Supabase database that only our servers can reach. Brief submissions are also delivered to us as a notification through Netlify Forms, the service that hosts this website.We use Google Analytics to understand how the site is used — which pages are visited and which actions are taken, such as opening or submitting the brief form. Google Analytics sets cookies in your browser and processes this data on Google's infrastructure. It does not receive the contents of your brief.These providers operate in the United States and elsewhere, so your information may be processed outside your country.How long we keep itWe keep a project brief for as long as it takes to answer it and to maintain a record of the conversation, and product update registrations until you ask to be removed. You can ask us to delete either at any time.Your choicesYou can ask for a copy of what we hold about you, ask us to correct it, or ask us to delete it. Write to contact@sourcinglabusa.com and we will action it.You can block analytics cookies in your browser settings or with a content blocker. The site works normally without them.ContactQuestions about this notice go to contact@sourcinglabusa.com.Back to the brief form
